clinicalPearls: Sympathetic paragangliomas arise from extra-adrenal chromaffin tissue along the paravertebral and para-aortic sympathetic chain, most commonly in the abdomen
Catecholamine excess produces episodic or sustained hypertension with the classic triad of headache, palpitations and sweating
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating elevated plasma or urinary metanephrines rather than measuring catecholamines directly
A high proportion are hereditary, with succinate dehydrogenase (SDHx) mutations, particularly SDHB, being the most important predisposing genes
SDHB-related tumours carry a notably higher risk of malignant, metastatic behaviour
Functional imaging with gallium DOTATATE positron emission tomography is highly sensitive for localisation and detecting metastatic disease
Adequate alpha-adrenergic blockade must precede any surgery or biopsy to prevent a catecholamine crisis
Germline genetic testing and lifelong surveillance are recommended given the strong hereditary component and multifocal potential
reference.pathophysiology: Sympathetic paragangliomas are catecholamine-producing tumours derived from chromaffin cells of the extra-adrenal sympathetic paraganglia. Unregulated synthesis and release of noradrenaline and adrenaline (and their metabolites, the metanephrines) drive the cardiovascular and metabolic manifestations of catecholamine excess. A large fraction are linked to germline mutations, especially in the succinate dehydrogenase complex genes, which impair cellular oxygen sensing and mitochondrial metabolism and promote a pseudohypoxic tumorigenic state. SDHB mutations in particular confer a heightened tendency to metastatic spread.
additionalDifferentials: Essential hypertension with anxiety or panic disorder
Parasympathetic (head and neck) paraganglioma, typically non-secretory
additionalInvestigations: Plasma free or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines
Cross-sectional imaging of chest, abdomen and pelvis to localise the tumour
Functional imaging such as gallium DOTATATE positron emission tomography
Germline genetic testing including the succinate dehydrogenase genes
Chromogranin A as an adjunctive tumour marker
Cardiac and blood-pressure assessment before intervention
redFlags: Hypertensive crisis with headache, chest pain or arrhythmia
Metastatic disease, especially with an SDHB mutation
Precipitation of a crisis by unblocked surgery, biopsy or certain drugs
Family history suggesting a hereditary paraganglioma syndrome
reference.prognosis: Completely resected localised tumours, after appropriate perioperative adrenergic blockade, generally have a favourable outlook, but SDHB-associated and metastatic disease carries a worse prognosis and mandates long-term, often lifelong, biochemical and imaging surveillance.
pitfalls: Proceeding to surgery or biopsy without adequate preoperative alpha-blockade, risking a catecholamine crisis
Relying on catecholamine measurement instead of metanephrines and missing intermittently secreting tumours
Failing to offer germline genetic testing given the high heritability
Underestimating the malignant potential of SDHB-related tumours
Assuming a single lesion when disease may be multifocal
management: Complete surgical resection is the definitive treatment for localised disease
Mandatory preoperative alpha-adrenergic blockade with phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin followed by beta-blockade, with volume and salt loading, to prevent intraoperative hypertensive crisis
Systemic therapy for metastatic disease with I-131 MIBG or lutetium-177 DOTATATE radionuclide therapy, cytotoxic chemotherapy or external-beam radiotherapy
Long-term biochemical surveillance with plasma or urinary fractionated metanephrines to detect recurrence or metastasis
Germline genetic testing including the succinate dehydrogenase genes, with genetic counselling
Cascade screening of at-risk relatives given the high heritability
Management within an endocrine and endocrine-surgery multidisciplinary team
